title: Falls to Flu: 9 Winter Safety Tips for Seniors
summary: Winter safety tips for seniors: spot hypothermia, heat your home safely, prevent falls on ice, prepare for outages, and stay healthy through flu season.
body_markdown:
The most important winter safety tips for seniors come down to three things: stay warm, stay steady on your feet, and stay healthy. That means dressing for the cold, using heaters safely, clearing ice before it causes a fall, and having a plan for storms and power outages. GoGoGrandparent can help with the parts that are hard to do alone, like snow shoveling, rides on icy days, and prescription delivery.


Few things rival the beauty of a snowy winter morning, but the season brings real challenges. Frigid temperatures, icy sidewalks, and unpredictable weather all affect senior safety. With a little preparation, you can stay safe and comfortable all winter. Here are nine practical safety tips for seniors, from falls to flu season.


## **1. Know the signs of hypothermia**


As we age, it can get harder to notice when the body is getting too cold. Hypothermia happens when body temperature drops too low, and according to[MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/hypothermia.html) , "a body temperature below 95 °F (35 °C) is a medical emergency." Older adults are among those most at risk.


Hypothermia can make you sleepy, confused, and clumsy, and because it comes on gradually, you may not realize you need help. If you or someone you know seems unusually drowsy, confused, or unsteady after being in the cold, call 911 right away.


Frostbite is the other cold-weather danger to watch for, and it usually starts with the fingers, toes, nose, and ears.[Ready.gov](https://www.ready.gov/winter-weather) lists the signs as "numbness, white or grayish-yellow skin, firm or waxy skin." Numb skin can't warn you when it's getting worse, so if you notice any of these signs, get indoors and call your doctor or seek medical care. The best protection is covering every bit of skin you can before you head out, and coming back inside before your hands and feet start to hurt.


It also helps to have someone checking in. During a cold snap, a quick daily call with a family member, friend, or neighbor is an easy way to make sure everyone is warm and doing well. If you live alone, ask someone to be your cold-weather buddy, and offer to do the same for them.


## **2. Dress for the cold when you go out**


A few simple habits keep the cold from getting the upper hand when you're outside:


- **Check the forecast before you go.** Wind makes cold air feel much colder, so a sunny day with strong wind can be harder on the body than a still, cloudy one.
- **Limit time outdoors** on very cold or windy days, and run errands at the warmest part of the day, usually late morning or early afternoon.
- **Tell someone where you're going** if you'll be out walking alone, and carry a charged phone.
- **Dress in warm layers.** Layers trap warm air close to your body. Add a hat, scarf, warm socks, and gloves.
- **Wear a waterproof coat and boots.** Wet clothes pull heat away from your body fast.
- **Change out of damp clothes** as soon as you get home.
- **Keep a blanket in the car** in case you get stuck or the heat takes a while to kick in.
- **Warm up gradually when you come in.** A warm drink and a dry sweater help, and it's worth sitting a few minutes before you dive back into chores.
- **Ask your doctor about your medications.** Some medicines and health conditions affect how well your body stays warm.


## **3. Keep your home warm and draft-free**


Staying warm inside matters just as much as staying warm outside. Keep your home heated, especially overnight, and a programmable thermostat makes that easier. Heavy curtains help hold in heat, and closing the doors to rooms you don't use keeps the warmth where you spend your time.


A few everyday habits help too:


- **Open curtains on sunny days** to let the sun warm the room, then close them at night.
- **Layer your bedding** with flannel sheets or an extra blanket, and keep your bedroom adequately heated overnight.
- **Wear warm layers indoors,** like thermal tops, socks, and a sweater.
- **Keep moving.** Light activity such as a short walk around the house or a few gentle stretches helps you feel warmer.
- **Have warm meals and drinks.** Soups, stews, oatmeal, and tea are easy ways to warm up from the inside.


Drafts around doors and windows let cold air in, and small fixes make a big difference. ## **4. Use heaters and fireplaces safely**


When the temperature drops, it's tempting to crank up every heat source in the house. Heaters and fireplaces need a little care, so a few safety rules are worth following every time:


- **Give space heaters room.** The[Consumer Product Safety Commission](https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2023/CPSC-Warns-Consumers-to-be-Cautious-When-Using-Space-Heaters-Furnaces-and-Fireplaces-This-Winter) says to place them "at least three feet away" from drapes, furniture, and bedding. Plug electric space heaters directly into a wall outlet, never an extension cord or power strip. Turn them off before going to sleep or leaving them unattended, as the CPSC's[heater safety sheet](https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/heaters.pdf) advises.
- **Never heat your home with a stove or oven.** They aren't built for it and can create carbon monoxide.
- **Check your carbon monoxide alarms.** The CPSC recommends alarms "on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas."
- **Have the chimney inspected** before you light the first fire of the season.
- **Follow the instructions** for electric blankets and heating pads, and don't fall asleep with a heating pad on.


## **5. Get ready for power outages**


Winter storms can knock out heat, light, and refrigeration. The best time to prepare is before the first storm of the season, when stores are stocked and roads are clear. Ready.gov's advice is to "gather supplies in case you need to stay home for several days without power," and that's a good way to think about it: plan for a few days at home, not a few hours.


It's also worth sitting down with a family member or neighbor in the fall and talking through what you'll each do if a big storm hits. Who checks on whom, who has a spare room with heat, and where's the spare key? Five minutes of planning now saves a lot of worried phone calls later.


A little preparation keeps an outage from becoming an emergency:


- **Keep flashlights and batteries handy.** Skip candles, which are a fire risk.
- **Charge your phone before a storm,** and keep a portable charger ready.
- **Plan for medications and medical equipment.** Talk with your doctor and pharmacist ahead of time about what to do if the power goes out, and refill prescriptions before a storm hits.[GoGo prescription delivery](https://www.gogograndparent.com/services/prescription-delivery) can bring them to your door.
- **Use generators outdoors only.** Place them at least 20 feet from the home, with the exhaust pointed away from nearby buildings, the CPSC says. Never run one inside a home, basement, shed, or garage.
- **Keep an emergency kit** with water, non-perishable food, blankets, a first-aid kit, and a battery-powered radio.
- **Keep the fridge closed** as much as you can so food stays cold longer.
- **Write down important numbers** on paper, like family, your doctor, your pharmacy, and your utility company, in case your phone dies.
- **Have a plan for where to go.** If your home gets too cold, know whether you can stay with family or a neighbor until the power comes back.


## **6. Prevent falls outside**


Ice and snow make falls one of the biggest winter risks to senior safety, and a fall can mean a serious injury and a long recovery. Falls are common all year long: among adults 65 and older, "more than one out of four older people falls each year," according to the[CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/falls/data-research/facts-stats/index.html) . Winter adds slick steps, icy driveways, and early darkness to the mix. A few steps lower the risk:


- **Wear boots with non-skid soles** and good traction.
- **Add ice tips to your cane or walker** for a better grip on slick surfaces.
- **Keep walkways shoveled and salted.** This is a job worth handing off. GoGoGrandparent's home services include snow shoveling for walkways, steps, and driveways. Availability depends on your area, so call1 (855) 464-6872 and press 8 to check yours.
- **Take your time.** Short, flat steps are steadier on ice than long strides.
- **Stock up on ice melt early.** Buy salt or ice melt before the first storm, and keep it by the door so it's easy to reach.
- **Use the most sheltered entrance.** If one door gets more snow and ice than another, use the safer one for the season.


Shoveling deserves its own warning. Heavy, wet snow is hard work, and Ready.gov advises that you "reduce the risk of a heart attack by avoiding overexertion when shoveling snow." If you have a heart condition or haven't been very active lately, talk with your doctor before you pick up a shovel. If you do clear a small patch yourself, push the snow instead of lifting it, take breaks, and stop if you feel tired, short of breath, or unwell. For driveways and long walkways, handing the job to someone else is the safer choice.


Even with good preparation, slips happen. Carry your phone in a pocket rather than a bag when you go outside, so you can reach it if you fall. If you're hurt or can't get up safely, call 911.


If you hit your head, see your doctor right away, especially if you take blood thinners. And if you fall but feel fine, tell your doctor anyway, because a fall is worth talking through even when nothing seems broken.


## **7. Prevent falls inside**


Shorter days and wet boots bring their own risks indoors. These home modifications for seniors help:


- **Clear walkways** of clutter, cords, and furniture that sticks out.
- **Add grab bars and handrails** in the bathroom and on stairs.
- **Improve lighting,** especially in hallways and near stairs.
- **Use non-slip mats** at the entryway, where snow and water get tracked in.
- **Secure loose rugs** with rug tape, or remove them.
- **Wear grippy socks or non-slip slippers** on hardwood and tile floors.
- **Add night lights** between the bedroom and bathroom for trips in the dark.
- **Keep everyday items within easy reach** so you aren't climbing on a step stool in the middle of winter.


For a room-by-room walkthrough, see the[home safety checklist for older adults](https://www.gogograndparent.com/blog/the-ultimate-elderly-home-safety-checklist-for-aging-loved-ones) .


## **8. Skip the icy drive**


Winter driving is hard on everyone. If roads are unsafe, postpone nonessential trips. When conditions allow travel and you'd rather leave the driving to someone else,[GoGoGrandparent's senior rides](https://www.gogograndparent.com/services/rides-for-seniors) can help: you call1 (855) 464-6872 and press 0, and an operator arranges a ride with a highly-rated driver. You can book ahead for appointments, with no app or smartphone needed.


If you do drive, winterize your car first: check the tires, battery, brakes, and antifreeze. Keep the gas tank full, slow down, and leave extra space between you and the car ahead. It's also smart to keep a small winter kit in the trunk with a warm blanket, a hat and gloves, a flashlight with extra batteries, an ice scraper, a small shovel, water, a few snacks, and a phone charger that works in the car.


If a storm catches you on the road, Ready.gov's advice is simple: "If trapped in your car, then stay inside." Your car is shelter and makes you easier for rescuers to find. Call for help, stay buckled in with your coat and blanket on, and let someone know where you are. This is also why it helps to tell a family member your route and when you expect to arrive before any winter drive.


## **9. Stay healthy through cold and flu season**


Winter brings more colds and flu, so a few everyday habits are worth the extra effort. These senior health tips are simple:


- **Wash your hands often.** The[CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/about/index.html) says to scrub "for at least 20 seconds," and to use a hand sanitizer with "at least 60% alcohol" when soap isn't available.
- **Avoid touching your face,** especially your eyes, nose, and mouth.
- **Stay home when you're sick,** and keep some distance from people who are.
- **Clean frequently touched surfaces** like doorknobs, light switches, and remotes.
- **Talk with your doctor** before the season starts about the best ways for you to stay healthy this winter.
- **Rest, drink plenty of fluids, and eat well.** Fruits, vegetables, and whole grains are a good base for meals all winter.


Staying healthy in winter also means staying connected. Cold weather and early sunsets can keep people inside for days at a time, and that can feel isolating. Schedule regular calls with family or friends, plan a weekly coffee date, or join an indoor class at a senior center or library. ## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What body temperature signals hypothermia?**


A body temperature below 95 °F is a medical emergency, according to MedlinePlus. Older adults can lose body heat without noticing, so keep your home warm and dress in layers outdoors.


### **How can seniors prevent falls in winter?**


Wear boots with good traction, add ice tips to canes or walkers, keep walkways shoveled and salted, and improve lighting inside your home.


### **Can GoGoGrandparent help with snow shoveling?**


GoGoGrandparent can help arrange snow shoveling for walkways, steps, and driveways, depending on local availability. Call1 (855) 464-6872 and press 8 to check availability at your address.


### **How far should a space heater be from furniture?**


The Consumer Product Safety Commission says at least three feet away from drapes, furniture, and bedding.
